Notebook 5: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Answers Grounded in Your Documents

Dr Simon Hatzesberger
Programme slot: 10:55–11:15 CET

  Notebook 05_rag.ipynb of the repository https://github.com/simonhatzesberger/genai-beyond-the-basics-20261207

A model knows only what it was trained on, up to its cut-off date. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) retrieves the relevant passages from your own documents at question time and gives them to the model together with the question, so that the answer is grounded in a source you control and can cite. The use case extracts key figures from an insurer's 458-page annual report.

Contents

  1. Concept and purpose
  2. Setup
  3. Use case: extracting KPIs from an annual report with RAG
  4. Further applications and resources

1. Concept and Purpose

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines LLMs with external data sources to produce responses that are not only linguistically coherent but also factually grounded. The core principle behind RAG is that instead of relying entirely on knowledge embedded within the model, it selectively accesses external resources—such as databases, document repositories, or APIs—whenever specific and up-to-date information is required.

By integrating the natural-language strengths of LLMs with the precision of external data sources, RAG helps produce outputs that are:

  • Current, as external information can be continuously updated and seamlessly incorporated.
  • Accurate, by directly accessing relevant, authoritative data sources rather than relying on generalized knowledge.
  • Flexible, because new data sources can be quickly added or existing sources easily updated, allowing dynamic adaptation to changing information needs.

The implementation of a typical RAG workflow consists of five main stages, as illustrated in the figure below:

  1. Indexing (Chunking, Vectorize & Store)

    • Source materials (e.g., actuarial reports, policies, or regulations) are segmented into smaller, manageable pieces ("chunks"). This enables precise, targeted retrieval.
    • Each chunk is transformed into a semantic vector, mathematically representing its meaning in a high-dimensional space. These vectors are stored in a specialized, optimized data structure (such as a vector database) that allows rapid and accurate retrieval.

  2. Vectorize & Search

    • The user query is similarly transformed into a semantic vector, capturing its meaning and intent.
    • A search algorithm compares this query vector against the stored document vectors, identifying the most semantically similar chunks using an appropriate similarity metric, ensuring highly relevant retrieval results.

  3. Retrieve

    • Based on the query-vector comparison, the system fetches the most relevant chunks or documents from the vector database. These retrieved documents contain information directly applicable to the user's query.

  4. Augment

    • The original query, retrieved chunks, and any additional contextual instructions or system prompts are combined into an enriched prompt. This augmented prompt provides the LLM with both the user's question and the necessary external context for accurate answering.

  5. Generate

    • The LLM processes the enriched prompt, synthesizing the retrieved external information with its inherent linguistic and contextual understanding, ultimately producing a coherent, informative, and contextually relevant response.

By following this structured approach, RAG enables actuaries to leverage the interpretative capabilities of LLMs alongside continuously updated domain-specific data, ensuring outputs remain precise, compliant, and fully aligned with current actuarial practice.


Schematic illustration of the individual phases of RAG.
[Source: https://ai.plainenglish.io/a-brief-introduction-to-retrieval-augmented-generation-rag-b7eb70982891]

Note

RAG is an emerging field, yielding new approaches like GraphRAG from Microsoft, which extends RAG by also incorporating a knowledge graph representing semantic relations between relevant entities, or AgenticRAG approaches, where the query generation is improved by an underlying agent.

def load_openai_api_key(name: str = "OPENAI_API_KEY", file_path: str = "openai_api_key.txt") -> str | None:
    """Look for the key in Colab Secrets, then in an environment variable, then in a local text file."""

        if value:

    if os.getenv(name):

    for candidate in (Path(file_path), Path("..") / file_path):

    return None

3. Use Case: Extracting KPIs from an Annual Report with RAG

In this use case, we demonstrate how Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can be used to extract key performance indicators (KPIs) from annual reports of insurance companies, for example to enable cross-company comparisons.
The approach is intentionally generic and can be adapted to other document types as well, such as insurance conditions or regulatory filings.

The following three-stage RAG workflow illustrates the overall process:



Schematic illustration of the three-stage RAG approach for extracting KPIs from insurance company annual reports.
Source: Own illustration.

We use the Annual Integrated Report and Consolidated Financial Statements 2025 of the Generali Group (458 pages, published on generali.com). The PDF is downloaded at run time and not redistributed with this notebook. Before we start, we define the models and the parameters of the RAG system.

In [3]:
EMBEDDINGS_MODEL = "text-embedding-3-small"   # USD 0.02 per 1M tokens (as of 22 Nov 2026)

CHUNK_SIZE = 2000   # characters per chunk
OVERLAP = 300       # characters shared by neighbouring chunks, so a sentence cut at a border is not lost
TOP_N = 5           # number of chunks given to the model per question

GENERALI_ANNUAL_REPORT_2025 = ("https://www.generali.com/doc/jcr:b569c750-290c-4868-9b6f-655e0349451c/Annual%20Integrated%20Report%20and%20Con"
                               "solidated%20Financial%20Statements%202025_Generali%20Group_final.pdf/lang:en/Annual_Integrated_Report_and_Consolidated_Financial_Statements_2025_Generali_Group_final.pdf")

Stage 1: Preprocessing¶

Stage 1 is done once per document: download the PDF, extract the text page by page, clean it, cut it into overlapping chunks, and turn every chunk into an embedding, a vector of 1,536 numbers that represents its meaning. We keep the PDF page number of every chunk, so that every answer can be traced back to its source page.

In [4]:
def load_pdf_pages(url: str) -> list[str]:
    """Download a PDF into memory and return the text of each page."""
    resp = requests.get(url, headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (EAA training notebook)"}, timeout=120)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    with pymupdf.open(stream=resp.content, filetype="pdf") as doc:
        return [page.get_text() for page in doc]


def clean_text(text: str) -> str:
    """Collapse repeated spaces and drop empty lines."""
    text = re.sub(r"[ \t]+", " ", text).strip()
    return re.sub(r"\n\s*\n", "\n", text)


def create_chunks(text: str, chunk_size: int = CHUNK_SIZE, overlap: int = OVERLAP) -> list[str]:
    """Split a text into overlapping chunks of chunk_size characters."""
    if chunk_size <= overlap:
        raise ValueError("chunk_size must be greater than overlap.")
    return [text[i:i + chunk_size] for i in range(0, len(text), chunk_size - overlap)]


pages = load_pdf_pages(GENERALI_ANNUAL_REPORT_2025)
chunks = [{"page": p, "content": chunk}
          for p, page_text in enumerate(pages, start=1)
          for chunk in create_chunks(clean_text(page_text)) if len(chunk) > 200]
print(f"{len(pages)} pages, {sum(len(p) for p in pages):,} characters -> {len(chunks):,} chunks")

458 pages, 1,515,508 characters -> 1,053 chunks

Embeddings are requested in batches (several hundred chunks per API call), which takes seconds instead of minutes. The whole report costs about one cent to embed.

In [5]:
def embed(texts: list[str], batch_size: int = 256) -> np.ndarray:
    """Embeddings for a list of texts, as a matrix with one unit-length row per text."""
    vectors = []
    for i in range(0, len(texts), batch_size):
        resp = client.embeddings.create(model=EMBEDDINGS_MODEL, input=texts[i:i + batch_size])
        vectors += [d.embedding for d in resp.data]
    m = np.array(vectors)
    return m / np.linalg.norm(m, axis=1, keepdims=True)


chunk_vectors = embed([c["content"] for c in chunks])
print("Embedding matrix:", chunk_vectors.shape)
pd.DataFrame(chunks).sample(2, random_state=1)

Embedding matrix: (1053, 1536)

Stage 2: Prompt Augmenting¶

Stage 2 runs once per question: the question is embedded in the same way, compared with every chunk by cosine similarity, and the best-matching chunks are attached to the prompt. We define three questions that need different kinds of answers: a single figure with a label, a table of variable length, and a qualitative list.

In [6]:
queries = {
    "solvency_ratio": "What is the Generali Group's Solvency II ratio at 31 December 2025, in percent?",
    "discount_rates": ("Which discount rates (EUR, risk-free plus illiquidity premium or similar) did the group use for "
                       "insurance contract liabilities at 31 December 2025, by maturity in years?"),
    "climate_risk": "How does the group identify, measure and manage climate-change and natural-catastrophe risks?",
}

def retrieve(question: str, top_n: int = TOP_N) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The top_n chunks most similar to the question, with page and cosine similarity."""
    q = embed([question])[0]
    scores = chunk_vectors @ q                      # cosine similarity (all vectors have unit length)
    best = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:top_n]
    return pd.DataFrame([{**chunks[i], "similarity": round(float(scores[i]), 3)} for i in best])

retrieved = {key: retrieve(q) for key, q in queries.items()}
retrieved["solvency_ratio"][["page", "similarity", "content"]]

Check what was retrieved before relying on an answer. If the relevant passage is not among the top chunks, the model cannot answer the question correctly from them.

Stage 3: Response Generation¶

The final stage combines the question, the retrieved chunks (each labelled with its page) and an output schema per question. The model is told to use only the snippets, to cite the pages it used, and to say when the snippets do not contain the answer.

In [7]:
class SolvencyRatio(BaseModel):
    solvency_ratio_percent: float | None = Field(description="Solvency II ratio in percent, null if not stated")
    regulatory_framework: Literal["Solvency II", "other", "not stated"]
    source_pages: List[int]

class DiscountRate(BaseModel):
    maturity_years: int
    rate_percent: float

class DiscountRates(BaseModel):
    currency: str
    rates: List[DiscountRate]
    source_pages: List[int]

class ClimateRiskManagement(BaseModel):
    measures: List[str] = Field(description="One short bullet per measure, process or control")
    source_pages: List[int]

SCHEMAS = {"solvency_ratio": SolvencyRatio, "discount_rates": DiscountRates, "climate_risk": ClimateRiskManagement}

RAG_INSTRUCTIONS = """You extract information from snippets of an insurer's annual report for actuarial analysis.
Use only the snippets provided. Each snippet starts with its page number; list the pages you used in source_pages.
If the snippets do not contain the requested information, return null or empty values instead of guessing."""

def answer_with_rag(key: str):
    snippets = "\n\n".join(f"<snippet page={r.page}>\n{r.content}\n</snippet>"
                            for r in retrieved[key].itertuples())
    response = client.responses.parse(
        model=MODEL, reasoning=REASONING, instructions=RAG_INSTRUCTIONS,
        input=f"Question: {queries[key]}\n\nSnippets:\n{snippets}",
        text_format=SCHEMAS[key],
    )
    return response.output_parsed

results = {key: answer_with_rag(key) for key in queries}
for key, result in results.items():
    print(f"=== {key}\n{result.model_dump_json(indent=2)}\n")

Checking the answer against its source¶

Because every answer carries its source pages, a reviewer can verify it in seconds. The cell below prints the lines of the cited pages that contain the reported solvency ratio.

In [8]:
sr = results["solvency_ratio"]
if sr.solvency_ratio_percent is not None:
    needle = f"{sr.solvency_ratio_percent:g}"
    for p in sr.source_pages:
        hits = [line.strip() for line in pages[p - 1].splitlines() if needle in line]
        print(f"page {p}: {hits[:3] or 'value not found verbatim on this page'}")

page 178: ['At year-end 2025, the solvency position of the Group is confirmed solid, with the Solvency Ratio at 219% (210% at 31 December', '219%']

What to take from this¶

  • Stage 1 (indexing) is done once; stages 2 and 3 cost fractions of a cent per question.
  • Retrieval quality decides answer quality: chunk size, overlap, the embedding model and the wording of the question all matter. Inspect retrieved chunks while developing.
  • Ask for evidence (pages, quotes) in the schema and check it in code. A RAG answer without a source is just another model answer.
  • Annual reports contain several similar figures (group vs. subsidiaries, regulatory vs. economic, prior year vs. current year). Say precisely which one you mean.

4. Further Applications and Resources

Additional Actuarial Use Cases for Retrieval-Augmented Generation¶

  • Market-Comparison Intelligence – A RAG pipeline pulls KPIs from annual reports, rating agency releases, and tariff brochures, letting actuaries benchmark premiums, loss ratios, etc. against competitors in real time.
  • Data-Migration Support – During system conversions, RAG retrieves and cross-checks policy attributes from both the legacy and the new platform, helping identify missing or conflicting fields before cut-over.
  • Internal Knowledge Hub – Employees can query thousands of underwriting manuals, regulatory circulars, and training decks; RAG fetches the most relevant passages and the LLM crafts concise answers—boosting findability and onboarding speed.
  • Real-Time Risk Alerts – By continuously ingesting news feeds and supervisory updates, a RAG agent flags emerging catastrophe events or regulatory changes that could impact reserve adequacy or solvency capital.

Further Reading and Resources on Retrieval-Augmented Generation¶

  1. Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey — Gao et al. (2024)
    • Type: Survey Paper
    • Summary: The standard RAG survey; frames the Naive / Advanced / Modular RAG paradigms and the retrieve–augment–generate pipeline.
  2. Vector embeddings — OpenAI API Guide
    • Type: Official Documentation
    • Summary: Current text-embedding-3-large / -small, the dimensions parameter, and search/RAG usage.
  3. Introducing Contextual Retrieval — Anthropic (2024)
    • Type: Engineering Guide
    • Summary: Prepend LLM-generated context to each chunk before embedding (plus BM25) to cut retrieval failures substantially.
